Yes I believe it was, speaking as a Brit with an amateur knowledge of nuclear strategy and a good understanding of what was known at the time. Some of you will debate me, and I honour you for showing the stubbornness needed to defend your views, but it's relatively clear from utilitarian ethics and the military knowledge possessed by both sides that dropping the bombs was at least partly justified, even if only because the bombings killed far less people than an actual invasion would have, on both sides.

Firstly, The circumstances of the situation meant that an invasion of mainland Japan was still likely on the cards. The Japanese government was debating a conditional surrender at the time the first bomb was dropped, and there was a significant contingent among them who were absolutely intent on carrying on the war rather than admitting defeat, regardless of how incapable they were of actually winning it. Moreover, the Americans knew that the Japanese would stoop to what could be described as incredibly barbarous lows in order to deprive the enemy of victory, partly from the fighting in the Pacific campaign and partly from the inhuman treatment that Allied POWs got both in Burma and the Pacific. The shocking level of cruelty on part of the Japanese army, combined with the fanaticism that the government tried to foist on its civilian population, meant that an invasion of the mainland would have been an incredibly bloody affair for both sides. Roosevelt can be at least partly excused for taking the option of ending the war with an excessive show of force, given what he knew.

Secondly, The understanding of nuclear weapons at the time was almost non-existent. Given how quickly the first bombs were manufactured after the initial successful detonation, it was incredibly clear that the Americans viewed them solely as strategic super-bombs, as no-one really knew anything of the more ghastly effects of an atomic explosion. The Americans arguably viewed them as simply very powerful bombs at this point in time, and did not understand the lingering effects that such a bomb would have on both people and the environment. Therefore, they can arguably be excused of the more ghoulish effects of the bombings, as they simply did not know of nuclear fallout and had no idea of the things it would do aside from very merely destroying an entire city. In addition, the fact that they detonated in the air as opposed to exploding upon contact with the ground rendered the blasts somewhat less destructive than they would have been otherwise, creating little lasting effects simply because the airborne detonation spread both the fallout and the explosion itself across a much wider area.

Thirdly, Hiroshima and Nagasaki were chosen as targets for the mere fact that both of them were significant logistical hubs for the Japanese military. Though they did possess relatively large civilian populations, their main importance to both sides of the conflict was both of the cities were critical parts of the logistical system that supplied the Japanese army. The intent of the bombings was to coerce the Japanese into an absolutely certain surrender, not to kill vast numbers of enemy civilians. Besides, the Allies had been carrying out strategic bombing campaigns against German military infrastructure for quite some time before the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Given the aforementioned ignorance possessed by America about the environmental effects of the bombs, it was arguably viewed as no different from a conventional bombing of military infrastructure, differing only in the level of firepower used. Though many civilians did die in the bombings, the primary target of the bombs were the infrastructure and logistics that made up a huge chunk of the Japanese military capability, not the civilian inhabitants.

In conclusion, I think it was morally justified to bomb Hiroshima and Nagasaki, if only for the fact that the bombings prevented a conventional land invasion that would have likely lead to far more deaths on both sides than the amount of deaths caused by both of the bombings. I admit that there may have been a possible ulterior motive in regards to the threat of Soviet military force in the east, and that there may have been a better option than immediately wiping out two densely populated areas vis a vis how they were deployed, but that still doesn't really change the fact that the potential casualty numbers of a full invasion were simply far too large to not justify trying to use overwhelming force to scare the enemy into surrender. Though it was not the optimal solution to the problem of ending the war in the Pacific, it was not some Hollywood spectacle, and it is disingenuous to say that they should have gone for the minimal option when we have the dual benefits of hindsight and formerly confidential military data. Reality isn't some Hollywood movie where the dashing hero can take a third option where nobody has to die. A large part of statecraft is choosing the least horrible of your available outcomes, minimizing the damage when outright avoiding it is impossible. Bombing Hiroshima and Nagasaki may not have been the right choice, but it was the best possible choice to make in a situation where it was impossible to make the right choice.

The preparation on this one is quite minimal. It most involves forming the burgers themselves and getting all your toppings and condiments ready.

Here are some possibilities

  • Lettuce: tear into chunks that will fit onto a burger

  • Tomato: slice into rounds.

  • Avocado: Cut in half and slice thin.

  • Bacon: just drop them in a pan and cook until they reach the desired crispness.

  • Cheese: any kind you like

  • Pickles

  • Mayo

  • Ketchup

  • Mustard

  • anything else you may want.

You will want to season your meat before you form them into patties. There are all kinds of options here but the most basic will be just some salt and pepper.

The best method I have found to form patties is to grab a chunk of hamburger roll it into a ball and squash it down until it's flat. Note that depending on the type of meat you use i.e. the fat content. The most fat there is the more your burgers will shrink down when they cook. So if you are using 20% fat or higher, be sure to make them a bit bigger. Wash rinse repeat.

You can either cook them on the BBQ or on a stove top with a pan. The key is to ensure that they are cooked throughout and to your liking. Make sure you pan or grill is nice and hot and drop them on.

The finger check method is the best way to judge how done your meat is. See Here

Once your cooking surface is ready, drop them onto the grill. DO NOT SMASH THEM DOWN! just drop them and let them cook. Note that if you notice juice starting to pool on the top flip them immediately, if you wait this long then your burgers will be more on the well done side. I usually wait about five minutes, when the bottom edges start to brown up.
